subtype: Approach: generates a big list first and judges it afterwards [Action]
passage: The Class 5 group had one rule on the back bench: nobody says no yet. Maria held the smudged notebook while Pema called out ideas, and the others followed. A talking crow. A lost tiffin box. A king who hates mangoes. Nobody laughed at the strange ones, and by the time the bell rang for lunch the page held twenty lines. After the break they read the list again. Anything needing a real boat or a cart full of props got a line drawn through it, since the stage was small. Maria counted what was left and circled three: the crow, the tiffin box and the mango king. They would try each one out on Friday.

qa.q: How many lines did the page hold when the bell rang for lunch?
qa.a: The page held twenty lines when the bell rang for lunch.

qa.q: What was Pema probably feeling while calling out the strange ideas?
qa.a: Pema was probably feeling free and excited, since nobody laughed and the ideas kept coming.

qa.q: What other way could the group pick their final three, and why might it work?
qa.a: After the cutting, each child could put a small tick beside a favourite, which gives everyone a say while the small stage still limits the choice.

qa.q: How might a classmate whose boat idea was crossed out see this plan?
qa.a: They might feel a little let down at first, but could accept it because every idea was written down and the reason was the small stage.

grounding: Shows a group listing many ideas first, then removing those that need too many props and keeping three.

subtype: Approach: generates ideas alone before sharing so early voices do not dominate [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Jaya,

You asked how the first club meeting of the year went, so here is the honest version. Last year I noticed the loudest three people always decided everything, so this time I handed out slips and said: five minutes, total silence, write anything. It felt strange. Nobody looked at anybody. Then we read the slips aloud with no names. Tashi, who has hardly spoken since joining in July, had written: a quiz round where teams pick their own topics. Half the room said yes at once. I had been nervous the meeting would drag, but it ended early and we chose that quiz. I think I will keep the silent five minutes.

Dolma

qa.q: What had Tashi written on the slip?
qa.a: Tashi had written a quiz round where teams pick their own topics.

qa.q: How was Dolma feeling when the silent five minutes began?
qa.a: Dolma felt strange and a little nervous, because nobody looked at anybody and Dolma feared the meeting might drag.

qa.q: What could Dolma do if a member still found it hard to share a slip?
qa.a: Dolma could keep reading the slips aloud without names, or let members drop slips in a box first, so each idea is judged on its own. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tashi have experienced that meeting?
qa.a: Tashi may have felt surprised and encouraged, since the idea was heard without having to speak over louder members.

grounding: Shows a captain having members write ideas silently before discussion so a quiet member's idea is chosen.

subtype: Approach: criticises ideas during the generating phase and cuts the flow [Pitfall]
passage:
Note, Tuesday session, fest planning group. I sat at the back as agreed. Imran answered nearly every idea with "That will never work." Jaya offered a silent-disco stall and got that reply; the next suggestion, a rooftop film night, got it too. By the fifth idea the room had gone quiet. The list on the board ended up as a chai stall, a quiz and tug-of-war, all things done last year. Jaya stopped looking up from the phone. Afterwards I spoke with Imran alone and asked what he was trying to protect. He said he did not want the fest to flop. I suggested holding all judging back for a second round next week, and I will open the session with that rule.

Faculty advisor

qa.q: Which three ideas ended up on the board?
qa.a: The board ended up with a chai stall, a quiz and tug-of-war.

qa.q: What was Imran worried about, according to what he told the advisor?
qa.a: Imran was worried that the fest would flop, which explains why he shot down each idea.

qa.q: What went wrong in the session, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Judging every idea as it was spoken made people stop offering them, so only safe ones were left. Collecting ideas first and judging later, as the advisor plans for next week, could fix it.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt after the silent-disco stall was dismissed?
qa.a: Jaya probably felt discouraged and a bit embarrassed, which fits with looking down at the phone and going quiet.

grounding: Shows constant criticism during a brainstorm silencing the group so only familiar ideas reach the list.

subtype: Approach: separates a generation round from a selection round with agreed criteria [Revision]
passage: Sat in on Thursday's planning call for the onboarding project. The first twenty minutes went nowhere: each idea was picked apart the moment it was spoken, and Hansa, who had started to suggest a checklist, trailed off. Seema, the product manager, paused the call and told the group they would take ten minutes to throw out ideas with no comments at all. A timer went up on the screen. Fourteen ideas appeared. Then Seema wrote three headings: how much it costs, how long it takes, and whether users need it. The team scored each idea against them one by one. Four candidates survived, and Hansa's checklist was one of them. Seema plans to run the two rounds again next sprint, and I will sit in again.

qa.q: How many ideas appeared during the timed round?
qa.a: Fourteen ideas appeared.

qa.q: What was Seema probably thinking when the call stalled?
qa.a: Seema probably felt concerned that ideas were being killed too early, which is why Seema paused the call and brought out the timer and the no-comments rule.

qa.q: What could a team try if loud voices still took over the ten-minute round?
qa.a: Everyone could write ideas silently on notes first and then share them, so quieter people get in before any discussion starts.

qa.q: How might Hansa have seen the two-round method?
qa.a: Hansa may have felt relieved and valued, since the checklist was heard and then survived the scoring.

grounding: Shows a product manager separating a no-criticism idea round from a scoring round using agreed criteria.

subtype: Approach: reframes the problem to use an unexpected feature [Thinking]
passage: Sit, Shalini. This old man, Akash, once lost a ball beneath the old sofa. I was nine. My arm went in up to the shoulder and my fingers touched nothing but dust. My sister was giggling at me. Then I stopped asking myself, how do I reach it, and I asked, does my hand have to be the one that gets it? The ball only had to come out. So I ran to my school bag, pulled out my long steel ruler, lay flat on the floor, and pushed the ball gently sideways until it rolled into the light. It is funny, beta. The sofa never changed. Only my question did.

qa.q: What did Akash use to get the ball out?
qa.a: Akash used the long steel ruler from the school bag to push the ball gently sideways until it rolled into the light.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling with an arm under the sofa, touching only dust?
qa.a: Akash was frustrated, and probably a little embarrassed with the sister giggling nearby.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Akash changed the question from how to reach the ball to what would get it out, which opened up the idea of pushing it with a ruler.

qa.q: How might the sister have seen it when the ball rolled out?
qa.a: The sister, who had been giggling, may have been surprised and impressed that a ruler solved it after the reaching failed.

grounding: Shows Akash changing a stuck reach into a push and using a ruler from the school bag.

passage:
Science fair prep, Wednesday, second period. Tarun has been stuck at the back of the lab for two days because the school has no table big enough for his volcano-and-village model. Today he stood beside it muttering, "Models go on tables, so I need a giant table. But the fair gave everyone only one small one." I asked only, "Where is it written that it has to sit on a table?" He stared at the wall behind him. Then he said quietly, "Nobody wrote that. I just assumed it. If I build it flat on a board, the board can hang from the wall hooks." He is now sketching where the hooks would go and has gone to ask the lab assistant how much weight they can take.

Kalyani, science teacher

qa.q: What did the teacher ask Tarun?
qa.a: The teacher asked, where is it written that it has to sit on a table.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling while muttering beside the model?
qa.a: Tarun was frustrated and stuck, since two days had passed without a table big enough.

qa.q: What could Tarun try if the wall hooks cannot hold the board?
qa.a: Tarun could build the model in smaller sections or ask for another display spot, checking the real limit first rather than assuming.

qa.q: How might another student at the fair, who only has a small table, see Tarun's plan?
qa.a: That student might see it as clever and a relief, since it uses wall space and leaves more table room for others.

grounding: Shows a student questioning an assumed need for a big table and realising the model can hang from the wall.

subtype: Approach: changes the question from making it faster to removing the step [Action]
passage:
Hrithik: the attendance sheet at the workshop desk is a mess again 😅
Lakshmi: want two of us on copying it into the laptop after? we could type faster
Hrithik: I keep asking why we copy at all
Hrithik: made a form last night. everyone scans a QR code at the door and it lands straight in the sheet
Lakshmi: so no names to read out, no typing at midnight?
Hrithik: none. printed the code, taped it to the door
Lakshmi: I'll stand there Saturday and help anyone whose phone won't scan
Hrithik: yes please. paper sheet stays as backup
Lakshmi: 👍 last workshop we left after nine. maybe we get home for dinner this time
Hrithik: that's the plan

qa.q: Where did Hrithik tape the printed code?
qa.a: Hrithik printed the code and taped it to the door.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling about the copying routine?
qa.a: Hrithik was frustrated with the copying step and wanted to be rid of it, not just make it quicker.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi and Hrithik do so nobody is left out by the QR system?
qa.a: They could keep the paper sheet as a backup and have someone at the door to help anyone whose phone won't scan, as Lakshmi offers.

qa.q: How might an attendee without a working phone see the new check-in?
qa.a: They might feel awkward at first, but a volunteer at the door and a paper backup let them sign in without fuss.

grounding: Shows a volunteer removing the copying step of an attendance sheet with a QR check-in instead of speeding it up.

subtype: Approach: turns a clever reframe into a plan that ignores practical limits [Pitfall]
passage:
Mentor note, week 3, Kavitha's delivery project. The problem was that parcels sat at the gate because residents were out at work. Kavitha's new idea is a barter network: neighbours take in each other's parcels and swap favours such as cooking or tutoring. It is a genuinely interesting reframe, and Kavitha pitched it with energy. But when I asked how many neighbours had been asked, the answer was none. Twelve flyers were already printed and a sign-up form was live, yet nobody had discussed trust, such as who holds a key or what happens when a parcel goes missing. Two weeks of effort and the printing money went in before a single neighbour was asked. Next session we will go through what a small first trial would need.

Ankita

qa.q: How many flyers had already been printed?
qa.a: Twelve flyers were already printed.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be feeling about the barter idea?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably excited and proud of the reframe, given the energy in the pitch.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do instead of printing more materials?
qa.a: Kavitha could ask a few neighbours whether they would trade favours and trust each other with parcels, and try it small before spending more.

qa.q: How might a neighbour who was never asked see the flyer?
qa.a: They might feel unsure or wary, since nobody had explained who holds a key or what happens if a parcel goes missing.

grounding: Shows a clever reframe turned into a full plan without testing whether people would take part or trust it.

subtype: Approach: keeps the fresh idea and tests it with one small pilot [Revision]
passage: Bao read Nadia's barter plan twice and said only, "It's a nice idea, but nobody has tried it." Nadia was stung for a minute, then opened her notebook. She did not drop the idea. Instead she picked one lane, the one with fourteen doors, and told the neighbours she would run it for two weeks. A shared shelf by the corner shop held parcels, and a paper sheet listed favours on offer. By day six people used the shelf happily, but nobody signed the favour sheet. Neighbours said writing favours down felt like keeping accounts. On day ten Nadia swapped the sheet for a thank-you jar and a weekly chat over tea. At the end she wrote down what people accepted and what they had not, and began planning the next lane.

qa.q: How many doors did the lane have?
qa.a: The lane had fourteen doors.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel when Bao said nobody had tried the plan?
qa.a: Nadia was stung for a minute, so hurt, but not defeated, since she opened her notebook and kept the idea.

qa.q: What else could Nadia try to learn more about the favour sheet problem?
qa.a: She could ask a few neighbours what would make swapping favours feel comfortable, since the shelf worked and only the written sheet did not.

qa.q: How did the neighbours see the favour sheet?
qa.a: Neighbours felt writing favours down was like keeping accounts, which made a friendly swap feel more like a debt.

grounding: Shows a person keeping a fresh idea, testing it in one lane for two weeks and adjusting from what people accepted.

subtype: Approach: postpones a heated decision until emotions settle [Action]
passage:
'Your message came at ten past seven,' Elizabeth said, sliding into the seat across from Samir in the library. 'Can we talk at lunch? That's all it said.'

'Yeah.' Samir rubbed the back of his neck. 'I wrote a much worse one last night after the match. Whole paragraph. It's still in my drafts.'

'You didn't send it?'

'I wanted to. My thumb was right there. But I put the phone under the pillow and went to sleep.'

'Why?'

'Everything I wrote sounded like winning, not fixing. This morning I just wanted to hear your side.'

Elizabeth gave a small laugh. 'I was ready to fight, honestly. I had a whole speech.'

'Then let's hear it.'

'Okay. But I go first.'

'Go.'

qa.q: At what time did the short message arrive?
qa.a: The message came at ten past seven and asked whether they could talk at lunch.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as his thumb hovered over the angry draft?
qa.a: Samir was angry and tempted to send it, wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: What else could Samir do if waiting a night had not cooled things?
qa.a: Samir could write his side down privately or take a walk before contacting Elizabeth, or ask someone he trusts how to start the talk.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth probably feel when the short message arrived?
qa.a: Elizabeth had been ready to fight, so the short message likely came as a surprise and a relief that softened the mood.

grounding: Shows a teenager drafting an angry message, waiting a night, and sending a calmer note asking to talk.
